content: 1. QTc prolongation has been reported with doses of fostemsavir exceeding the recommended levels. Close monitoring is advised when fostemsavir is co-administered with drugs like sorafenib, sotalol, sunitinib, tacrolimus, telavancin, terbutaline, tetrabenazine, thioridazine, triclobendazole, triptorelin, vandetanib, vardenafil, vemurafenib, voriconazole, vorinostat, ziprasidone, and others that also increase the QTc interval. Caution should be exercised in these cases. 2. St. John’s Wort is contraindicated with fostemsavir as it decreases fostemsavir levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism, potentially leading to loss of virologic response and resistance. 3. Co-administration of fostemsavir with strong CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., enzalutamide, carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampin, mitotane, St. John’s Wort) is contraindicated as it significantly reduces the plasma concentration of temsavir (the active moiety of fostemsavir), risking virologic failure. 4. Fostemsavir inhibits BCRP and OATP1B1/3 transporters, which can increase the plasma levels of substrates like sulbactam, sulfasalazine, talazoparib, telmisartan, troglitazone, valsartan, velpatasvir, voxilaprevir, and zavegepant. Dose adjustments or alternative therapies should be considered, and close monitoring is recommended. 5. Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) has been reported with combination antiretroviral therapy, including fostemsavir. This may manifest as an inflammatory response to latent or residual opportunistic infections (e.g., Mycobacterium avium, cytomegalovirus, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, or tuberculosis) and may require further evaluation and treatment. Autoimmune disorders (e.g., Graves’ disease, polymyositis, Guillain-Barré syndrome) have also been reported. 6. Liver enzyme monitoring is recommended in patients co-infected with hepatitis B or C virus, as elevated hepatic transaminases have been observed more frequently in these individuals. Effective hepatitis B therapy should be maintained or initiated when starting fostemsavir to prevent hepatitis B reactivation. 7. The Antiretroviral Pregnancy Registry (APR) encourages clinicians to register pregnant patients exposed to fostemsavir by calling 1-800-258-4263. Human data on fostemsavir use during pregnancy are insufficient to assess the risk of birth defects or miscarriage. 8. The CDC advises HIV-1–infected mothers in the United States not to breastfeed to prevent postnatal transmission of HIV-1. It is unknown if fostemsavir is excreted in breast milk, affects milk production, or impacts breastfed infants. 9. Fostemsavir tablets should be swallowed whole and not chewed, crushed, or split. They can be taken with or without food. Store at 20–25°C (68–77°F), with excursions permitted to 15–30°C (59–86°F). Tablets may have a slight vinegar-like odor. 10.
